title: Shortest Mirror by Prepending
statement:
You get a string s. You may add characters only to the front of it. Return the shortest string you can build this way that reads the same forwards and backwards.

The answer is unique: for a given length there is only one possible palindrome ending with s.

examples.why: "aba" at the front is already a palindrome, so only the trailing "c" needs a mirror copy in front.
"abba" sits inside the string but not at its start, so it does not help. The longest palindrome starting at index 0 is "aa", and the reversed "bba" goes in front.
Only the single "a" is a palindromic start, so the other three letters are mirrored.

hints: Whatever you add, the original s ends the result. Which part of s must already be a palindrome, and what do you add for the rest?
Find the longest prefix of s that is a palindrome. The answer is the reverse of everything after it, followed by s. Checking each prefix directly is O(n²) in the worst case.
A prefix of s is a palindrome exactly when it equals a suffix of reverse(s). Build s + '#' + reverse(s) and compute the KMP failure function: its last value is the length of the longest such prefix.

explain.intuition:
The result ends with all of s, and the added part must mirror whatever of s is not already symmetric. So the job is to find the longest palindromic prefix of s; the answer is the reverse of the leftover tail, followed by s.

A prefix p of s is a palindrome exactly when p also appears as a suffix of reverse(s). "Longest prefix that is also a suffix" is precisely what the KMP failure table computes. Run it on s + "#" + reverse(s); the separator stops a match from running across the middle. The table's last entry is the length you want, in linear time.
steps: Build the failure table: fail[i] is the length of the longest proper prefix of t[0..i] that is also its suffix.
Let k = fail[t.length − 1]: the longest palindromic prefix of s has length k.
pitfalls: Using the longest palindrome anywhere in the string. It must start at index 0, as "aabba" shows.
Leaving out the separator. Without it, for "aa" the table can match more than s.length characters.
Assuming the quadratic prefix check is fine on random input. Strings like a…ab a…a make every check run deep before failing.

solutions.title: Check prefixes from longest to shortest
solutions.idea: Try each prefix length from n down; the first palindrome found is the longest one.

solutions.title: KMP failure table on s # reverse(s)
solutions.idea: The longest palindromic prefix is the longest prefix of s that is also a suffix of reverse(s), which the failure table gives directly.

followups: Solve it with a rolling hash of the prefix read forwards and backwards. What is the risk, and how do you remove it?
Characters may be added only at the end instead. What changes?
